content: 1. The usual starting dose of Glucophage (metformin hydrochloride tablets) is 500 mg taken twice daily or 850 mg taken once daily, administered with meals. 2. Dosage increases should be made in increments of 500 mg weekly or 850 mg every two weeks, up to a total daily dose of 2000 mg, given in divided doses. 3. Patients may also be titrated from 500 mg twice daily to 850 mg twice daily after two weeks. 4. For patients requiring additional glycemic control, Glucophage may be administered up to a maximum daily dose of 2550 mg. 5. Doses exceeding 2000 mg may be better tolerated when given three times daily with meals. 6. The usual starting dose of Glucophage XR (metformin hydrochloride extended-release tablets) is 500 mg once daily with the evening meal. 7. Dosage increases should be made in increments of 500 mg weekly, up to a maximum of 2000 mg once daily with the evening meal. 8. If glycemic control is not achieved with Glucophage XR 2000 mg once daily, a trial of Glucophage XR 1000 mg twice daily should be considered. 9. If higher doses of metformin are required, Glucophage should be used at total daily doses up to 2550 mg, administered in divided doses as described above. 10. In a randomized trial, patients treated with Glucophage were switched to Glucophage XR. 11. Results from this trial suggest that patients receiving Glucophage may be safely switched to Glucophage XR once daily at the same total daily dose, up to 2000 mg once daily. 12. Following the switch from Glucophage to Glucophage XR, glycemic control should be closely monitored, and dosage adjustments should be made accordingly. 13. When transferring patients from standard oral hypoglycemic agents (other than chlorpropamide) to Glucophage or Glucophage XR, no transition period is generally necessary. 14. When transferring patients from chlorpropamide, caution should be exercised during the first two weeks due to the prolonged retention of chlorpropamide in the body, which may lead to overlapping drug effects and potential hypoglycemia. 15. If patients have not responded to four weeks of the maximum dose of Glucophage or Glucophage XR monotherapy, gradual addition of an oral sulfonylurea should be considered while continuing Glucophage or Glucophage XR at the maximum dose, even if prior primary or secondary failure to a sulfonylurea has occurred. 16. If patients do not respond satisfactorily to one to three months of combined therapy with the maximum dose of Glucophage or Glucophage XR and the maximum dose of an oral sulfonylurea, therapeutic alternatives should be considered, including switching to insulin with or without Glucophage or Glucophage XR. 17. The current insulin dose should be continued when initiating Glucophage or Glucophage XR therapy. 18. Glucophage or Glucophage XR therapy should be initiated at 500 mg once daily in patients on insulin therapy. 19. For patients not responding adequately, the dose of Glucophage or Glucophage XR should be increased by 500 mg after approximately one week and by 500 mg weekly thereafter until adequate glycemic control is achieved. 20. The maximum recommended daily dose is 2500 mg for Glucophage and 2000 mg for Glucophage XR. 21. It is recommended to reduce the insulin dose by 10% to 25% when fasting plasma glucose concentrations decrease to less than 120 mg/dL in patients receiving concomitant insulin and Glucophage or Glucophage XR. 22. Further adjustments should be individualized based on the glucose-lowering response. 23. Glucophage or Glucophage XR is not recommended for use during pregnancy or in pediatric patients. 24. Initial and maintenance dosing of Glucophage or Glucophage XR should be conservative in elderly patients due to the potential for decreased renal function in this population. 25. Any dosage adjustment should be based on a careful assessment of renal function. 26. Generally, elderly, debilitated, and malnourished patients should not be titrated to the maximum dose of Glucophage or Glucophage XR. 27. Monitoring of renal function is necessary to help prevent lactic acidosis, particularly in elderly patients.
